specStatements.text: Photosynthesis is represented by the equation:
Students should recognise the chemical symbols: CO2 , H2 O, O2 and C6 H12 O6 .
Students should be able to describe photosynthesis as an endothermic reaction in which energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.
Students should be able to explain the effects of temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, and the amount of chlorophyll on the rate of photosynthesis.

Students should be able to: measure and calculate rates of photosynthesis; extract and interpret graphs of photosynthesis rate involving one limiting factor; plot and draw appropriate graphs selecting appropriate scale for axes; translate information between graphical and numeric form.
These factors interact and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis.
Students should be able to explain graphs of photosynthesis rate involving two or three factors and decide which is the limiting factor.
Students should understand and use inverse proportion – the inverse square law and light intensity in the context of photosynthesis.
Limiting factors are important in the economics of enhancing the conditions in greenhouses to gain the maximum rate of photosynthesis while still maintaining profit.

The glucose produced in photosynthesis may be: used for respiration; converted into insoluble starch for storage; used to produce fat or oil for storage; used to produce cellulose, which strengthens the cell wall; used to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
To produce proteins, plants also use nitrate ions that are absorbed from the soil.

concepts.definition: The reaction represented by the equation carbon dioxide + water → (light) glucose + oxygen, which takes place in the chloroplasts. Written with chemical symbols, CO2 and H2O react to form C6H12O6 and O2.
A reaction that takes in energy from its surroundings. Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in which energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.
The amount of product formed in a given time, calculated by dividing the amount of product by the time taken, for example bubbles of oxygen released per minute or cm3 of oxygen produced per minute.

The factor that is controlling the rate of photosynthesis at that moment, so that increasing it increases the rate. Temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll all affect the rate of photosynthesis.

Temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll interact, and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. On a graph, the limiting factor is the one which, when increased on its own, raises the rate further.

concepts.term: inverse square law and light intensity
concepts.definition: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source. Doubling the distance reduces the light intensity to one quarter, and halving the distance increases it four times.

Growers enhance temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration in greenhouses to gain the maximum rate of photosynthesis. The cost of enhancing the conditions must be less than the extra income gained, so limiting factors are important in the economics of greenhouse growing.

The glucose produced in photosynthesis may be used for respiration, converted into insoluble starch for storage, used to produce fat or oil for storage, used to produce cellulose which strengthens the cell wall, or used to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
Ions that are absorbed from the soil and used by plants, together with the glucose produced in photosynthesis, to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.

misconceptions.question: Is photosynthesis an endothermic or an exothermic reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in which energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.
misconceptions.misconception: Photosynthesis gives out energy, because it makes glucose and glucose is an energy store, so it must be an exothermic reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet glucose as the energy store used in respiration, so they assume that any reaction which produces glucose must release energy. The word 'light' written over the arrow is also read as a product of the reaction rather than as the energy that is taken in.
misconceptions.correction: Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction: energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light. Energy is taken in by the reaction, it is not given out.

misconceptions.question: Does raising the temperature always increase the rate of photosynthesis?
misconceptions.correct: Raising the temperature increases the rate only while temperature is the limiting factor; at high temperatures the enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured and the rate falls.
misconceptions.misconception: The warmer a plant is kept, the faster it photosynthesises, so raising the temperature increases the rate whatever the starting temperature is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students generalise from the rising part of a rate-temperature graph, and from the rule met in chemistry that heating makes reactions go faster. They forget that photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, which are denatured at high temperatures.
misconceptions.correction: Temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis. It increases the rate while it is the limiting factor, but above the optimum temperature the enzymes are denatured and the rate falls.

misconceptions.question: Why does a graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity level off?
misconceptions.correct: The rate levels off because light intensity is no longer the limiting factor; another factor, such as temperature or carbon dioxide concentration, is now limiting the rate.
misconceptions.misconception: More light gives more photosynthesis at every light intensity, so a flat graph means the plant has run out of water, or that the rate is still rising and the graph simply does not show it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Light is taught as the thing that drives photosynthesis, so students treat it as the only factor that matters and look for damage to the plant or a fault in the experiment to explain a flat line, instead of using the idea of a limiting factor.
misconceptions.correction: Light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis, but the factors interact and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. Where the graph is flat, a factor other than light intensity is limiting the rate.

misconceptions.question: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm away from a plant. What happens to the light intensity reaching the plant?
misconceptions.correct: The light intensity falls to one quarter of its value at 10 cm, because light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source.
misconceptions.misconception: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the distance itself, so doubling the distance from the lamp halves the light intensity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Inverse proportion is normally met as y being proportional to 1/x, so students apply simple inverse proportion to the distance and do not square it. Distances in centimetres are also used directly in the fraction instead of the change in distance.
misconceptions.correction: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source. Doubling the distance reduces the light intensity to 1/2 squared, which is one quarter.

misconceptions.question: What substance does photosynthesis produce, and in what form is it stored?
misconceptions.correct: Photosynthesis produces glucose. The glucose may then be converted into insoluble starch for storage.
misconceptions.misconception: Starch is what photosynthesis makes, and glucose and starch are two names for the same food store in a plant.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The iodine test for starch is used in class to show that a leaf has photosynthesised, so students conclude that starch is the direct product of the reaction and stop distinguishing it from the glucose in the equation.
misconceptions.correction: The equation shows that photosynthesis produces glucose (C6H12O6). The glucose produced may then be used for respiration, converted into insoluble starch for storage, used to produce fat or oil for storage, used to produce cellulose, or used to produce amino acids.

misconceptions.question: Where do the proteins in a plant come from?
misconceptions.correct: The plant makes them: glucose produced in photosynthesis is used with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
misconceptions.misconception: Plants take in ready-made protein from the soil through their roots, which is why fertiliser has to be added to the soil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fertiliser is described as 'plant food', so students picture the soil as supplying finished food substances such as protein, rather than ions that the plant uses to build molecules for itself.
misconceptions.correction: To produce proteins, plants use nitrate ions that are absorbed from the soil. These are used with the glucose produced in photosynthesis to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.

misconceptions.question: A student counts 90 bubbles of oxygen from pondweed in 3 minutes. What is the rate of photosynthesis?
misconceptions.correct: The rate is 30 bubbles per minute, because the rate is the number of bubbles divided by the time taken.
misconceptions.misconception: The rate of photosynthesis is the number of bubbles that were counted, so the more bubbles collected, the higher the rate, whatever the time taken.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students record the largest number in their results table and read it as 'how much photosynthesis happened'. Rate is not yet treated as a quantity measured per unit of time, so the time column is ignored or is multiplied in rather than divided by.
misconceptions.correction: Rate of photosynthesis is calculated as the amount of product formed divided by the time taken, for example bubbles of oxygen per minute or cm3 of oxygen per minute.

misconceptions.question: How does photosynthesis differ from respiration in a plant?
misconceptions.correct: In photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water are used to produce glucose and oxygen in the chloroplasts, with energy transferred from the environment by light. Plants also respire, and some of the glucose is used for respiration.
misconceptions.misconception: Photosynthesis is respiration in reverse, so a plant takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide when it photosynthesises, and plants photosynthesise instead of respiring.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two equations look like mirror images of each other, so reactants and products get swapped. Being told that plants 'give out oxygen' is also heard as 'plants do not use oxygen', and the site of each reaction is mixed up.
misconceptions.correction: Photosynthesis is represented by: carbon dioxide + water → (light) glucose + oxygen, and it takes place in the chloroplasts. The glucose produced in photosynthesis may be used for respiration, so plants carry out both reactions.

mcqs.stem: Which line shows the equation for photosynthesis written in chemical symbols?

options.text: CO2 and H2O react to form C6H12O6 and O2.
options.rationale: This is the equation carbon dioxide + water → (light) glucose + oxygen written with the chemical symbols CO2, H2O, C6H12O6 and O2.

options.text: C6H12O6 and O2 react to form CO2 and H2O.
options.rationale: A student who believes photosynthesis is respiration in reverse writes the equation the wrong way round. This line has glucose and oxygen as the reactants, which is respiration; in photosynthesis they are the products.

options.text: CO2 and O2 react to form C6H12O6 and H2O.
options.rationale: A student who believes a plant takes in oxygen while it photosynthesises puts O2 on the left. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, and water is a reactant, not a product.

options.text: CO2 and H2O react to form C6H12O6 and heat.
options.rationale: A student who believes photosynthesis gives out energy shows heat as a product. Photosynthesis is endothermic: energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light, and the second product is oxygen.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes photosynthesis as an endothermic reaction?

options.text: Energy is transferred from the chloroplasts to the surroundings.
options.rationale: A student who believes photosynthesis releases energy reverses the direction of transfer. An endothermic reaction takes energy in from the environment, it does not transfer energy out to it.

options.text: Energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts.
options.rationale: Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in which energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.

options.text: Energy is transferred from the surroundings to the mitochondria.
options.rationale: A student who mixes photosynthesis up with respiration names the wrong structure. Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, and energy is transferred to the chloroplasts by light.

options.text: Energy is transferred from the glucose to the environment as heat.
options.rationale: A student who believes making glucose must release its stored energy chooses an exothermic description. In photosynthesis the energy transferred in by light is used to make the glucose.

mcqs.stem: A student measures the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed by counting bubbles of oxygen. She counts 90 bubbles in 3 minutes. What is the rate of photosynthesis?

options.text: 30 bubbles per minute
options.rationale: Rate is the amount of product divided by the time taken: 90 bubbles ÷ 3 minutes = 30 bubbles per minute.

options.text: 90 bubbles per minute
options.rationale: A student who believes the rate is simply the number of bubbles counted gives the total. The total must be divided by the 3 minutes taken to give a rate per minute.

options.text: 270 bubbles per minute
options.rationale: A student who does not treat rate as an amount per unit time multiplies the count by the time instead of dividing by it. Multiplying gives a larger number than was actually collected in one minute.

options.text: 0.03 bubbles per minute
options.rationale: A student unsure which quantity to divide by does 3 ÷ 90 and inverts the calculation. This gives minutes per bubble, not the number of bubbles produced per minute.

mcqs.stem: A student plots the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed against light intensity at a constant temperature. The graph rises steeply and then becomes a horizontal line. Which statement explains the horizontal part of the graph?

options.text: Light intensity is still limiting the rate on the flat part.
options.rationale: A student who believes more light always gives a faster rate keeps light as the limiting factor. If light intensity were still limiting, increasing it would still be increasing the rate and the line would not be horizontal.

options.text: The plant has switched from photosynthesis to respiration.
options.rationale: A student who treats photosynthesis and respiration as alternatives thinks the plant swaps between them. The pondweed is still photosynthesising, at a steady rate set by whichever factor is now limiting.

options.text: The rate is still rising but the graph is not showing it.
options.rationale: A student who believes the rate must keep rising with light blames the graph. The horizontal line is real data showing that the rate has stopped increasing because another factor is limiting it.

options.text: Another factor, such as temperature, is now limiting the rate.
options.rationale: The factors interact and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. Once light intensity is no longer limiting, temperature or carbon dioxide concentration limits the rate, so the rate stops rising.

mcqs.stem: A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at 20 °C and at 30 °C, both at the same carbon dioxide concentration. Both curves rise and then become horizontal, but the 30 °C curve becomes horizontal at a higher rate. Which statement about the graph is correct?

options.text: Light intensity is limiting the rate where the 20 °C curve is flat.
options.rationale: A student who believes light is always the controlling factor keeps it as the limiting factor. Where the curve is flat, adding more light does not raise the rate, so light intensity is not the limiting factor there.

options.text: Temperature is limiting the rate on the steep part of each curve.
options.rationale: A student who believes temperature always controls the rate applies it to the whole graph. On the steep part the rate rises as light intensity rises, so light intensity is the limiting factor there.

options.text: Temperature is limiting the rate where the 20 °C curve is flat.
options.rationale: On the flat part, increasing light intensity has no effect, but raising the temperature to 30 °C gives a higher rate. The factor that raises the rate when it alone is increased is the limiting factor.

options.text: Raising the temperature to 50 °C would raise the flat part again.
options.rationale: A student who believes a higher temperature always gives a faster rate extends the pattern. At 50 °C the enzymes controlling photosynthesis would be denatured, so the rate would fall instead.

mcqs.stem: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from a piece of pondweed. Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the lamp. What happens to the light intensity reaching the pondweed?

options.text: It falls to 1/2 of the intensity at 10 cm.
options.rationale: A student who believes intensity is inversely proportional to distance halves it when the distance doubles. The distance must be squared, so the intensity falls by a factor of 2 squared, not 2.

options.text: It falls to 1/16 of the intensity at 10 cm.
options.rationale: A student unsure how the squaring works squares the correct factor of 4 a second time. The squaring is applied to the ratio of the distances, 2, giving a fall to one quarter.

options.text: It falls to 1/4 of the intensity at 10 cm.
options.rationale: The distance is doubled, so the light intensity falls by a factor of 2 squared: it becomes one quarter of the intensity at 10 cm.

options.text: It falls to 1/20 of the intensity at 10 cm.
options.rationale: A student applying simple inverse proportion uses the distance value of 20 cm directly. The inverse square law compares the two distances, so it is 1/2 squared that is needed, not 1/20.

mcqs.stem: How does a plant obtain the amino acids it uses for protein synthesis?

options.text: Amino acids are made from starch and nitrate ions.
options.rationale: A student who treats starch as the product of photosynthesis names it as the raw material. Photosynthesis produces glucose; starch is the insoluble form the glucose is converted into for storage.

options.text: Amino acids are made from glucose and nitrate ions.
options.rationale: Glucose produced in photosynthesis is used to produce amino acids, and to do this plants also use nitrate ions that are absorbed from the soil.

options.text: Amino acids are absorbed from the soil by the roots.
options.rationale: A student who believes the soil supplies ready-made food substances has the plant absorbing amino acids. Only the nitrate ions are absorbed from the soil; the amino acids are produced by the plant.

options.text: Proteins are absorbed from the soil by the roots.
options.rationale: A student who thinks of fertiliser as plant food has protein taken in whole. Plants produce their own proteins, using nitrate ions absorbed from the soil together with glucose from photosynthesis.
